books.section: Unit 5: Toward the Civil War and Reconstruction (1844–1877)

primary_sources: Harriet Beecher Stowe, Uncle Tom’s Cabin, 1852

stimulus.source_note: Harriet Beecher Stowe, Uncle Tom’s Cabin; or, Life Among the Lowly (Boston: John P. Jewett & Company, 1852), Chapter 40, "The Martyr". Public domain.
stimulus.text: The longest way must have its close — the gloomiest night will wear on to a morning. An eternal, inexorable lapse of moments is ever hurrying the day of the evil to an eternal night, and the night of the just to an eternal day.

source: original; stimulus as noted in stimulus.source_note
stem: Southern responses to Uncle Tom’s Cabin — including novels defending slavery and efforts to ban Stowe’s book — most directly show that Southerners saw the novel as

options.text: a work of history with no errors.
options.misconception: Southerners attacked the book, they did not praise its accuracy; their answers were novels and bans, not compliments.

options.text: a harmless entertainment with no political meaning.
options.misconception: A harmless book is not banned and not answered; the bans and the reply novels show the South took it seriously.

options.text: a dangerous attack on slavery that could sway the North.
proof that Northerners supported the Fugitive Slave Act of 1850.
options.misconception: Background from the books: the novel fed Northern anger at the Fugitive Slave Act; it showed opposition to the act, not support for it.

rationales.A: Southerners attacked the book, they did not praise its accuracy; their answers were novels and bans, not compliments.
rationales.B: A harmless book is not banned and not answered; the bans and the reply novels show the South took it seriously.
rationales.C: Banning a book and writing novels to answer it are the acts of people who fear what it will do to Northern minds.
rationales.D: Background from the books: the novel fed Northern anger at the Fugitive Slave Act; it showed opposition to the act, not support for it.
rationales.general:
1. List the Southern answers: bans on the book and novels praising slavery.
2. Ask what those answers cost: banning takes effort, and reply novels take time.
3. Read the effort as fear: the South answered because it believed the novel could move the North.
Remember: judge a book’s power by the energy spent answering it, not by its sales alone.
